papers.title_in_file: Generalized quantum geometric tensor for excited states using the path integral approach

papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that derives a path-integral formulation of the quantum geometric tensor for any energy eigenstate, extends it to translations of phase-space coordinates (which gives the quantum covariance matrix, purity and entropy for Gaussian states), shows it equals the Provost-Vallee and Zanardi forms, and computes metrics and scalar curvatures for oscillator systems.

the insights from which thus cannot be directly transferred to DP data.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not test whether insights from MNIST or CIFAR transfer; the assertion is a premise, not a result.

assertions.value: The authors state that training on all existing and newly arrived data from scratch in general ensures performance but requires storage of all the data and increasing computing resources at each update. They state that updating a model with transfer learning has no extra cost of data storage and computing resources but is known to suffer from catastrophic forgetting.
quotes: Such an approach in general ensures performance, but requires storage of all the data and an increasing amount of computing resources each time a model is updated
updating a model with transfer learning, albeit with no extra cost of data storage and computing resources, is known to suﬀer from catastrophic forgetting [14].
assertions.reader_inference: Motivation for the study. The forgetting claim is attributed to reference 14 (Kirkpatrick et al.).

assertions.value: The authors list three contributions: identifying continual learning scenarios practical for digital pathology analysis and characterizing the performance of recent CL methods in them; establishing an augmented H&E dataset simulating data streams from multiple data sources; and exploring learning continuously from more than one tumor type and applying online CL methods.
quotes: Our contributions are three-fold: (1) we identify continual learning scenarios practical for DP-based analysis
(2) we establish a dataset with augmented H&E images, simulating data streams from multiple data sources
(3) we have explored the feasibility and provided insights into performance of both learning continuously from more than one type of tumor
assertions.certainty_reason: The introduction states the scope of the study.

assertions.value: The authors state that they used a colorectal cancer (CRC) dataset of stain-normalized 224x224 patches at 20x from H&E stained whole-slide images (136 patients) with tile-wise labels for 9 tissue types: tumor, stroma, normal, lymphocyte-rich, mucin, muscle, adipose, debris and background.
quotes: composed of stain-normalized [18] 224x224 patches at 20x from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained wholeslide images (136 patients)
with tile-wise class labels for 9 tissue types - tumor, stroma, normal, lymphocyte-rich, mucin, muscle, adipose, debris, background.

assertions.value: The authors state that, to establish a class-balanced dataset, they randomly selected 8700 images from each class for training (7000 train; 2700 validation) and used the entire test set (7150 images) for testing.

assertions.reader_inference: The stated figures do not add up: 7000 plus 2700 is 9700, not 8700. The later text also uses 8700/5 = 1740 examples per class per domain 'for training', which would be 1400 if training were 7000. The paper does not say which figure is the actual training size.

assertions.value: The authors state that recent continual learning methods can be largely classified into replay, regularization and parameter isolation methods, citing reference 28. They state that parameter isolation methods only apply to Task-IL because they require multi-headed designs and use task IDs to select a task-specific head at inference, while replay and regularization apply to all scenarios.

while replay and regularization apply to all scenarios, parameter isolation only applies to Task-IL
both require multi-headed designs and use task IDs to select a task-speciﬁc head during inference.
assertions.reader_inference: Parameter isolation methods are not evaluated in the paper, consistent with its choice of scenarios.

assertions.value: The authors describe EWC and Online EWC as regularization-based methods whose loss includes a term penalizing large changes to network weights important for previous tasks, proportional to each weight's importance. They state that in EWC the number of quadratic penalty terms grows linearly with the number of tasks, and that Online EWC uses a single quadratic penalty term whose strength is determined by a running sum of parameter importance, with an additional decay hyperparameter.
quotes: The loss function includes a regularization term, which penalizes large changes to network weights that are important for previous tasks
In EWC, the number of quadratic penalty terms grows linearly with the number of tasks.
Online EWC [23] uses a single quadratic penalty term on parameters whose strength is determined by a running sum of parameter importance from previous tasks.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's description of methods proposed in references 14 and 23.

assertions.value: The authors describe LwF as a data-focused regularization method that distills knowledge from a previous model to an updated model trained on new data, replaying each input with a soft target obtained from a copy of the model stored after training on the most recent task.

Each input is replayed with a soft target obtained using a copy of the model stored after ﬁnishing training on the most recent task.

assertions.value: The authors define an experience as learning from a batch of data for CL. They report accuracy averaged over test sets at the end of training the last experience from multiple repeats, and accuracy over multiple repeats at each experience. They state that evaluation on test sets from past experiences indicates how well the model retains past knowledge without forgetting (backward transfer), while accuracy on current or future test sets reflects new knowledge assimilation (forward transfer).

accuracy averaged over test sets at the end of training the last experience from multiple repeats

accuracy on current/future test sets reﬂects new knowledge assimilation (forward transfer)

assertions.value: The authors state that all methods were compared against two baselines: joint training (upper bound), where a model was trained on all the data available so far, and finetuning (that is, transfer learning; lower bound), where a model was trained sequentially with exposure to only the data from the current experience. For A-GEM and CoPE they also compared online versions of the baselines: A-GEM baselines trained in an online setup for 1 epoch, and CoPE baselines with experiences divided into mini experiences of 128 samples each, trained for 1 epoch per mini experience.
